content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a severe genetic disorder caused by the inheritance of two abnormal beta-globin genes. This condition can lead to significant complications, including severe pain, damage to vital organs, pulmonary issues, and premature death. Individuals with SCD often require surgical interventions at younger ages compared to the general population. Preoperative blood transfusions are commonly used in these cases, but there is no consensus on the optimal transfusion strategy or whether transfusions are necessary for specific surgical procedures. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether preoperative blood transfusions reduce mortality and serious complications related to surgery or SCD. Additionally, it aimed to compare the effectiveness of different transfusion strategies, such as aggressive versus conservative regimens, in individuals with SCD undergoing surgery. Three trials involving 990 participants were included in this review. These trials were conducted between 1988 and 2011, and most participants had HbSS SCD. The majority of the surgeries were classified as low or intermediate risk for SCD-related complications. Aggressive versus Simple Transfusion Regimens One trial with 551 participants compared an aggressive transfusion regimen (reducing sickle hemoglobin to less than 30%) to a simple transfusion regimen (increasing hemoglobin to 100 g/L). Participants were re-randomized, so data analysis was limited to two subgroups: those undergoing cholecystectomy (230 participants) and those undergoing tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy (107 participants). The evidence quality was very low due to high risk of bias, lack of blinding, indirectness, and imprecise outcome estimates. Mortality: No deaths occurred in either subgroup, and there was no difference in all-cause mortality between the aggressive and conservative transfusion groups. Acute Chest Syndrome: There was no significant difference between the groups (risk ratio [RR] 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.38 to 1.84; very low-quality evidence). Vaso-occlusive Crisis: No significant difference was observed (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.04; very low-quality evidence). Serious Infections: No significant difference was found (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.59 to 5.18; very low-quality evidence). Perioperative Complications: No significant difference was noted (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.55; very low-quality evidence). Transfusion-related Complications: No significant difference was observed (RR 1.85, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.88; very low-quality evidence). Preoperative Transfusion versus No Preoperative Transfusion Two trials with 434 participants compared preoperative transfusion plus standard care to standard care alone. The evidence quality was low to very low due to high risk of bias and imprecise outcome estimates. One trial was stopped early because more participants in the no-transfusion group developed acute chest syndrome. Mortality: No deaths occurred in either group across the two trials. Acute Chest Syndrome: Results were inconsistent between the two trials. One trial showed a significant reduction in acute chest syndrome with preoperative transfusion (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.80; 65 participants), while the other trial did not (RR 4.81, 95% CI 0.23 to 99.61; 369 participants). A meta-analysis was not performed due to this heterogeneity. Vaso-occlusive Crisis: No significant difference was observed (Peto odds ratio [OR] 1.91, 95% CI 0.61 to 6.04; very low-quality evidence). Serious Infections: No significant difference was found (Peto OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.29 to 5.71; very low-quality evidence). Perioperative Complications: No significant difference was noted (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.03 to 2.05; low-quality evidence). Circulatory Overload: One trial reported an increase in circulatory overload in the preoperative transfusion group, while the other trial reported no events. A meta-analysis was not performed. Authors' Conclusions There is insufficient evidence from randomized trials to determine whether conservative preoperative transfusion is as effective as aggressive transfusion in preventing complications related to SCD or surgery in individuals with HbSS disease. Very low-quality evidence suggests that preoperative transfusion may reduce the risk of acute chest syndrome. However, due to the lack of robust evidence, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the management of individuals with HbSC or HbSβ+ disease or those with high baseline hemoglobin levels.
